o: Count integers in [1,n] with all distinct digits, n up to 2e9 (≤ 10 digits). Classic digit-DP/counting: first count all special numbers with fewer digits than n (for d digits: 9 choices for the leading digit × falling factorial of remaining choices), then walk n's digits left to right, counting completions that place a smaller unused digit at the first differing position, finally adding 1 if n itself is special. Example: n=20 → nine 1-digit numbers + numbers 10-19 with distinct digits (9 of them, excluding 11) + 20 itself = 19.
k: Numbers with d < len(n) digits: Σ 9 · P(9, d-1) where P is the falling factorial.
Prefix-matching phase: at each position, count unused digits smaller than n's digit, times permutations of the remaining slots from remaining digits.
Stop early if n's own prefix repeats a digit; add 1 at the end if n is fully distinct.

a.i: Handle shorter lengths wholesale, then mimic the digit-DP tight-path traversal: maintaining the set of used digits, for each position add (number of allowable smaller digits) × P(remaining_digits, remaining_slots). This counts every special number below n exactly once.
s: Walk n's digits; at position i (leading digit restricted to ≥1), add (#unused digits < s[i]) · P(10-used-1, L-i-1).
If s[i] was already used, break; otherwise mark it used.
If the loop completes, add 1 for n itself.
a.t: O(L²) with L ≤ 10 digits — the inner digit scans and falling factorials are bounded by 10.

w: Verify against small cases: n=5 → 5 (only the short-length term... actually L=1 so the loop adds 1 for n itself, total 5 ✓); n=20 → 19 ✓. Pitfalls: forgetting the leading digit can't be 0 in the short-length and first-position counts, forgetting to add 1 for n itself when it's special, and stopping the tight walk upon the first repeated digit. Follow-up: solve the general 'numbers with distinct digits in [l,r]' or memoized bitmask digit DP for arbitrary bounds.
